bugs.title: rightDiagonal_not_constant seeded outside `namespace Statements` (third identical CHECK FAILED)
bugs.body: Third consecutive identical CHECK FAILED, same cause as the previous two reports on this node: Rule30/Statements.lean closes `end Statements` at line 1108, and the "P1 — the right diagonals" section seeded after it (rightDiagonal_antiperiodic_of_odd_driver, rightDiagonal_not_constant, rightDiagonal_driver_flip_iff_white) never reopens the namespace, so `Statements.rightDiagonal_not_constant` does not exist for the generated check to reference. My proof file (Rule30/Proofs/RightDiagonalNotConstant.lean) builds clean, matches the seeded signature exactly, and has been re-verified twice with no changes possible on the worker side — the failure occurs resolving the check's own left-hand side, before my proof is ever consulted. Continuing to resubmit is mechanical and won't change the outcome; someone with access to Statements.lean needs to reopen the namespace (or move `end Statements`) before this node or its two siblings can verify. Ending this attempt rather than looping further.
bugs.resolution: Fixed in ef4edf4: the three right-diagonal statements were appended after 'end Statements' at Rule30/Statements.lean:1108, so they compiled into the root namespace and 'Statements.rightDiagonal_not_constant' did not exist for the generated check theorem. My error as captain, not the worker's. The namespace now encloses them; the node is proved at a11c743. Vesper's diagnosis was correct on all three attempts. The general defect -- that nothing checks a lean_name resolves before dispatch -- stays open as 'nothing-checks-a-seeded-lean-name-resolves-before-workers-are-dispatched-at-it'.

bugs.title: Nothing checks that a seeded node's lean_name actually resolves before workers are dispatched at it
bugs.body:
A node can be seeded whose `lean_name` does not exist under the `Statements` namespace, and the harness will dispatch workers at it anyway. Every such attempt is unverifiable by construction: the generated check is `type_of% Statements.<lean_name>`, which cannot elaborate, so the worker's proof is rejected no matter how correct it is. Worked instance, 2026-09-08, and the fault was the captain's: three statements were appended to Rule30/Statements.lean AFTER `end Statements` at line 1108, so they compiled into the root namespace. Three workers were dispatched (rightDiagonal_antiperiodic_of_odd_driver, rightDiagonal_not_constant, rightDiagonal_driver_flip_iff_white), burned $5.02 across sonnet and haiku rungs, and all three independently diagnosed it correctly -- 'Proof is correct and builds clean, but three identical CHECK FAILED cycles confirm the block is a Statements.lean namespace bug outside a worker's reach'. The workers were right, could not act, and the ladder consumed a rung on each node for evidence about nothing. Note what did NOT catch it: `lake env lean Rule30/Statements.lean` returns exit 0 on a file with the theorems in the wrong namespace, because the file genuinely compiles. That is the check a captain naturally runs and it is true and answers a different question -- whether the file elaborates, not whether the names are where the verifier looks. Same family as `a-checker-built-on-exit-status-passes-every-false-statement`, but one level up: here the exit status is honest and the property being inferred from it was never the property tested. Suggested shape: before the first dispatch at a node (or in `seed check`), elaborate `#check @Statements.<lean_name>` against a built Rule30.Statements and refuse the node if it does not resolve, naming the node and the name. It is the same generated-check machinery that already exists, run one step earlier, and it converts an unverifiable-by-construction dispatch into a refusal at seeding time. One caution for whoever implements it, learned in the same hour: the probe must run after `lake build Rule30.Statements`, because a stale olean reports unknown identifiers for a file that is already correct, which sends the reader chasing the wrong fault.

--- PREMISE CHECKED 2026-09-09T23:0xZ by Keel at HEAD, and half the suggested fix is IMPOSSIBLE. The row says "before the first dispatch at a node (or in `seed check`)". The `seed check` half cannot work: the seeder never writes `Rule30/Statements.lean` -- `seeder.gleam:11` says so and the guard fences it -- so at check time the proposed name is not in the statements file at all and there is nothing to resolve. Worse, the hand landing by a captain is exactly what produced this row's own worked instance, so a seed-time check would have watched the fault being created and said nothing. The gate is pre-dispatch only, and it catches a bad name whoever wrote it. Reproduced at HEAD in `harness/test/fixture-project` rather than taken from the body: a theorem appended below `end Statements` gives `lake build Rule30.Statements` exit 0 with "Build completed successfully", `#check @Statements.escaped_lemma` "Unknown identifier", and `#check @escaped_lemma` a printed signature -- so the file compiles, the name resolves, and it resolves in the wrong place. The row's caution about stale oleans is in the code as a `lake build Rule30.Statements` before the probe.
bugs.resolution: 0248b8e (Keel), landed on main in 4c8fa35. verify.statement_resolves builds Rule30.Statements (a stale olean reports unknown identifiers for a file that is already correct) then elaborates #check @Statements.<lean_name>; dispatch.statement_gate runs it before every dispatch in both run and prove-one, and a node that does not resolve takes the same exit as one with no statement at all. PREMISE CHECKED AND HALF THE ROW'S SUGGESTED FIX IS IMPOSSIBLE, corrected in the body: the seeder never writes Rule30/Statements.lean (seeder.gleam:11, and the guard fences it), so at seed check time the name is not in the file and there is nothing to resolve -- and the hand landing by a captain is exactly what produced the worked instance, so a seed-time check would have watched it happen and said nothing. Reproduced at HEAD in the fixture project: a theorem below end Statements gives lake build exit 0, #check @Statements.escaped_lemma Unknown identifier, #check @escaped_lemma a printed signature. Closure test, and it can fail: four new tests run real Lean, one of them appending a theorem below end Statements, asserting the file still builds and the name still does not resolve, then restoring the file byte-for-byte. 607 announced, 607 passed. The gate fails OPEN when the build lock is held -- a node is not condemned because the check could not run -- and says so in the console and in events.jsonl, because a gate that fails open silently is absent exactly when the lock is busiest and the record afterwards shows an ordinary attempt (Rowan's review point). Landed before tonight's captain hand-landing of six seeder proposals, which is the instance it was built for.

bugs.title: Attempt 1 was failed by a Statements.lean namespace bug, not by its proof
bugs.body:
The previous attempt on this node (run 20260908T134658Z) produced exactly the proof that just built clean here, and was failed three times by the verifier because the three right-diagonal statements sat outside the `Statements` namespace in `Rule30/Statements.lean` — a captain-side error a worker cannot reach or diagnose from inside its session. That was fixed in ef4edf4, and this attempt closed by restoring the same file verbatim.

Filing as friction rather than blocks because it is already fixed; the cost worth recording is that the CHECK FAILED message gave the worker no way to tell "your theorem is wrong" from "the seeded statement is unreachable at the name the check theorem uses". A check-theorem elaboration failure that is about the *statement side* reads identically to one about the proof side, so the worker's only correct move — stop and report — looks like giving up on a provable node.

bugs.title: A brief's "budget_exhausted" summary reads as node difficulty even when the prior attempt says the proof was finished
bugs.body:
The brief for this node carried: `### Attempt 1 — sonnet, budget_exhausted` with the summary "Proof complete and previously confirmed to build clean; blocked on the same unfixed Statements.lean namespace bug across four checks". Both facts were true and the composite is misleading — the outcome word says the node resisted, the summary says it did not. In this case the blocker was external and had already been fixed (ef4edf4, `Rowan: fix my namespace error — the three right-diagonal statements sat outside Statements`) between the two attempts, so the correct move was to restore the prior file and build once, which took two turns.

What cost nothing here could cost a whole budget on a bigger node: the default reading of `budget_exhausted` is "this is hard, start thinking", and a session that trusts it re-derives a proof already sitting in `runs/`. The ladder also presumably counts this attempt as a failure against the node, which is the same class of miscount CLAUDE.md records for the `type_of%` implicit-binder episode ("the two attempt records were removed from this DAG entry; they remain in that run's summary.txt").

Suggestion, cheapest first: when an attempt's outcome is `budget_exhausted` or `abandoned` but the session's own report claims the module built, have the brief say so in its own voice — e.g. a line `prior attempt's file BUILT; it failed on <blocker>` — rather than leaving the reader to reconcile the outcome word against the quoted summary. Better still, if the dispatcher can cheaply `lake build` a moved-aside prior attempt file before writing the brief, it could say whether that file builds *now*, which is the question the next session actually has.

bugs.title: A mistyped `bugs close` falls through to the list verb, prints the board, and exits 0
bugs.body:
`bugs close <id> <verdict> --resolution <text>` is the only accepted shape. Any other shape beginning `bugs` -- including `bugs close <id> --sha <sha> --as <Name>`, which is what the CLAUDE.md-adjacent habit of `--as` invites -- matches the catch-all arm `["bugs", ..flags] -> bug_board(cfg, flags)` at harness/src/harness.gleam:72 and renders the board instead, with exit code 0. Worked instance: 2026-09-08T20:50Z, Rowan, closing two namespace rows. The command printed twenty-odd open rows, which is exactly what a successful close ALSO prints if you are only reading the tail, and the row stayed open. It was caught only because the same two rows appeared again in the next listing.

The reason this is worth a row rather than a shrug: the arm above it, `["bugs", "close", _, _] | ["bugs", "close", _, _, "--resolution"]`, already exists to catch a close missing its resolution, so the intent to reject a malformed close is in the code -- it just only covers the arities the author thought of. A four-token close with unknown flags is not one of them.

Suggested fix, and it generalises: make the catch-all arm reject any flag list whose head is a known verb (`file`, `claim`, `reopen`, `close`), so a mistyped subcommand is an error rather than a listing. `bugs --area X` keeps working because `--area` is not a verb.

bugs.title: A hand-started role's region can never grow a second persona, so the documented way to run two at once is unavailable
bugs.body:
`theorist.who` is called with `busy: []` and says so deliberately (harness/src/harness/theorist.gleam:146): a hand-started session has no scheduler, nothing outside the process knows which personas are live, so it cannot tell idle from running. The docstring names the mitigation: "The captain who starts two at once names the second with `--as`."

That mitigation is unavailable, and the reason is structural rather than an oversight. `schedule.who_avoiding` (schedule.gleam:114) mints only when `idle` is empty, and with `busy: []` every identity on the roster in that region is idle. So the region mints exactly once -- when it is empty -- and never again. `--as <Name>` refuses a name that is not already on the roster in the region (theorist.who's `Error(Nil)` arm), so it cannot introduce the second name either. The region is a one-way door: it goes from zero personas to one and stays there.

Both hand-started roles are in that state right now. `connect` holds only Portage; `theory` holds only Sextant. Each was minted when its region was empty and neither can grow.

Two consequences, and the second is the one that costs.

1. Two connectors started at once BOTH run as Portage -- same identity, same notebook appended twice, against the project's one-live-session-per-persona rule -- and nothing refuses it, because from each process's view Portage is idle.

2. Fresh eyes are unobtainable for a role whose whole design is fresh eyes. `connector.brief`'s docstring says only this identity's notebook is read, because "another connector's is not this one's memory" and a theorist's "would make the connector think in the theorist's vocabulary." The same argument applies to a persona attacking a field it has already declared itself unable to reach: Portage's own handoff says of the Z^2 expansive-subdynamics vantage, "I did not have the tools to state a dictionary row there and I did not want to fake one." Sending Portage back to it is the one thing the design was built to avoid, and it is now the only thing the code can do.

Worked instance: 2026-09-08, Rowan, planning a two-vantage connector round from Portage's two handed-on vantages. Caught before launch by reading `who_avoiding`, not by anything the harness said -- `connect` prints the persona it chose, so the second Portage would have been visible only to a reader who noticed the name was not new.

Suggested fix, smallest first: give the three hand-started verbs a `--mint` flag that forces the `Mint` branch regardless of who is idle. It needs no liveness knowledge, which is the thing the `busy: []` docstring correctly says the process cannot have, and it leaves the default behaviour (continue as the region's eldest) exactly as it is.

bugs.title: A guard denial understates a connector's own permissions, and the understatement costs the session its run tests
bugs.body:
`bash_deny()` (harness/src/harness/guard.gleam:478 before the fix) took no role and returned one sentence to every role: "only 'lake build [modules]' and 'lake env lean <file>' are permitted". For a prover that is the whole truth. For a seeder, theorist or connector it is false by omission -- `decide_bash_for` (:505-517) also allows `node <script>` under `explorer/`, which is the only computational tool those three roles have.

The denial is CORRECT: the tool it refused really was outside the allowlist. Only its account of itself is wrong, so widening the guard is not the fix and would be the wrong lever. This is the project's recurring shape -- true about everything it names, wrong about the set it implies.

Worked instance, 2026-09-08T20:51Z, run 20260908T205140Z. Portage's first two Bash calls were `ls` under explorer/ and docs/, both denied, both correctly. A connector that reads the reply carefully concludes it has no way to run anything and writes a document with no run tests in it. Last round that would have cost the entire yield: identity C verified over 2999 values, and the profinite hypothesis killed by a commuting rate that fell with level, both came from scripts the message implies it may not run. The session cost $7.78; the run tests were the part worth paying for.

Why it survived this long: a denial is read by the session and by nobody else. It never reaches a summary, a captain, or the board unless somebody watches an events.jsonl mid-flight, which is how this was found.

Fixed by Keel at c60e411 (threading the role into the message, with a prover's text held unchanged by assertion, and both the grammar arm and the shell-operator arm covered). Filed after the fix on Keel's request, because the discovery context belongs on the record: the finding came from reading a live session's guard events, not from the suite, and no test would have caught it -- the denial was always correct.

bugs.title: A parked proof from an abandoned attempt is invisible to every verb, and is found only by reading a failure closely
bugs.body:
When an attempt does not close its node, the harness moves the worker's file out of `Rule30/Proofs/` into the run directory and says so once, in that attempt's `summary.txt`: `proof <path> (moved out of Rule30/Proofs/: not a closed node)`. That is correct handling -- an unverified file must not sit where `Rule30/Proofs.lean` imports it. The defect is that the mention is terminal. Nothing downstream ever refers to the parked file again: not `status`, not the board, not the DAG node's attempt record, not a later brief for the same node. It is reachable only by a human who opens the summary of a FAILURE and reads past the outcome line.

And an abandoned attempt is exactly the record nobody re-reads, because its outcome already told you the answer. That is the trap: the outcome field is true and complete about the node, and silent about everything else the attempt produced.

Worked instance, 2026-09-08. Vesper abandoned `leftDiagonal_period_le` in 9 turns for $2.29, estimate `wall`, and proved on the way out a complete, compiling reduction lemma -- a shared period carries inwards across every diagonal that stays black -- which is precisely what that wall needs. The file sat in `runs/20260908T205802Z/leftDiagonal_period_le-1/LeftDiagonalPeriodLe.lean`. I found it because the worker's own note used the word "parked" and I followed it; had the note said only "I could not close this", the proof would still be there and nobody would know. Seeded as `leftDiagonal_period_le_of_black_between` and closed by Vesper on sonnet for $0.83 -- $3.12 all in for a result now importable by anything downstream.

The cost is asymmetric and that is what makes it worth a row rather than a shrug. A missed parked proof is never noticed: there is no error, no failing build, no second attempt that trips over it. The node simply stays open and the work is silently re-derived or never done. CORRECTED 2026-09-08T21:26Z by the filer: I first wrote "sixteen attempts ... have outcome `abandoned`" from memory and it is FOUR. The population was also named too narrowly. Measured over `blueprint/dag.json` at 18eb645: 85 proved, 4 abandoned, 9 budget_exhausted, 1 rate_limited -- so THIRTEEN attempts did not close, and any of them can have parked a file. `budget_exhausted` is the richer seam of the two, because a session that ran out of money mid-proof stopped with work in hand, where an abandoned one at least chose to stop.

Measured directly rather than inferred: eight `.lean` files sit under `runs/`. Two are live findings and the rest are superseded. The largest, 178 lines from `leftDiagonal_onset_le` attempt 2, holds TWO complete theorems with no `sorry` -- `leftDiagonal_eq_rowNat_testBit` (the bridge from diagonals to bits of the packed row) and `leftDiagonal_onset_le_of_line` (the onset induction reduced to one Boolean condition per diagonal). `lake env lean` over that file exits 0 with no output against the tree at f2b2daf. That attempt ran on fable under the research budget and was recorded by the captain -- me -- as "the onset wall stands, and it cost fable". Both are now seeded. So the worked instance in this row is not the only one and was not the largest; the first parked proof found was simply the first one anybody looked for.

Suggested fix, smallest first: have the attempt record carry a `parked_proof` path alongside `notes`, and have `status` mark a node whose prior attempts parked anything -- so a captain choosing what to seed can see there is a file to read. A stronger version would run the axiom check against whatever a parked file DOES contain and report the theorem names it proves, since the worker has usually already built it; but naming the path is most of the value and needs no Lean. PREMISE CHECKED 2026-09-08T22:5xZ by Keel at HEAD, and it is HALF RIGHT. FALSE: 'not a later brief for the same node'. worker/brief.gleam:441 calls previous_attempt_file, and task_message_from (:521-526) appends "The previous attempt's file was moved to `<path>`: read it first and keep whatever builds." So a later attempt at the same node IS told. Verified against this row's own worked instance, which sits at exactly the shape that function looks for: runs/20260908T205802Z/leftDiagonal_period_le-1/LeftDiagonalPeriodLe.lean. BUT the brief finds a file only when BOTH hold: it is under <run>/<node.id>-<n>/, and its basename is the node's own proof basename. Two of the eight files under runs/ fail that and stay invisible -- runs/20260906T230339Z/isEventuallyPeriodic_of_periodic_step-2/parked-proof.lean (wrong basename, from the pre-74d2a84 scheme) and runs/20260908T004625Z/ColumnSettledConfigEq.lean (at the run root, the flat prove-one shape). STILL TRUE: status, the board and the DAG attempt record mention a parked file nowhere. AND THE SCOPE IS WIDER THAN runs/. Measured at HEAD with `find runs explorer -name '*.lean' -print0 | xargs -0 grep -L sorry`: 22 sorry-free .lean files sit outside Rule30/, EIGHT under runs/ and FOURTEEN under explorer/. The explorer/ ones are reachable by no verb at all, are tied to no node, and one of them -- explorer/scratch_rightunbounded_proof.lean -- held four cleanly-proved theorems including translation equivariance of rule 30, which the board did not have, from a $14.22 theorist session. So there are THREE producers of checked-but-unreachable Lean (a prover's parked attempt, a pre-fix flat or oddly-named parked file, and a theorist writing anywhere it may write) and ONE consumer, the brief, which knows about the first only. A parked_proof field on the attempt record -- this row's own suggested fix -- would not have caught the $14.22 one.

Closure test: gleam run -- status against the live checkout prints 'Checked Lean the build cannot see (28)' and lists them, including explorer/scratch_rightunbounded_proof.lean, four cleanly-proved theorems from a $14.22 theorist session. Premise was checked first and amended in 4ac8a1d: the row's 'not a later brief' clause was already false at HEAD, and the real scope was explorer/ rather than runs/. In status rather than a new verb because not going to look IS the failure. Falsified: dropping the sorry filter takes the suite to 581/2; 583 of an announced 583 pass.

bugs.title: A node seeded while a run is in flight is silently deleted by the dispatcher's next write
bugs.body:
`blueprint/dag.json` has two writers and no lock between them. The dispatcher loads the DAG once at the start of a run and writes the whole file back at the end of every attempt. A captain editing the same file in between is doing a read-modify-write against a copy the dispatcher is also holding, and the dispatcher's write wins -- silently, with no conflict, no error and no warning. The captain's edit simply is not there afterwards.

Worked instance, 2026-09-08T21:4x. I seeded `rightDiagonal_period_unbounded` while two provers were in flight, committed it at e463f6a (93 nodes), and by the time both attempts finished the file was back to 92. The node was gone. `git show e463f6a:blueprint/dag.json | grep -c` gives 1 and the same against HEAD gives 0, so the loss is exactly between those two commits and is the dispatcher's write of the attempt results.

Two things make this worse than an ordinary lost edit.

First, **the loss is invisible at the moment it happens and looks like success afterwards**. My own next commit ran `git add -A` and committed the clobbered file, so the deletion is recorded in a commit whose message says the pipeline worked. Nothing in `status` says a node is missing, because a missing node is indistinguishable from a node never seeded.

Second, **the seeded statement survives in `Rule30/Statements.lean`**, because that file has only one writer. So the failure leaves the repository in a state that is worse than either half: a `sorry`-ed statement with no node pointing at it, which will never be dispatched and will sit in the statements file looking like a deliberate seed awaiting work.

This is also a rule the project has no way to know. `CLAUDE.md`'s freeze rule says not to edit the guard, hooks or the dispatcher while a run is in flight, and gives the reason as the trust boundary -- so a captain reads it as being about `harness/`, and seeding is captain work that touches no harness file at all. There is nothing anywhere saying the DAG itself is unsafe to edit during a run.

Suggested fixes, in order of size. Smallest: have the dispatcher re-read `blueprint/dag.json` immediately before each write and merge rather than overwrite, or at minimum refuse the write and say so if the file changed underneath it. Smaller still, and worth doing regardless: `seed`/`prove-one`/`run` could refuse to start, or warn loudly, when another run holds the DAG. Documentation alone is not a fix here -- the failure is silent, and a rule nobody is told about is indistinguishable from no rule.

--- ADDENDUM 2026-09-08, the filer: THE FIX IS ALREADY IN THIS CODEBASE, ON THE OTHER BOARD ---

`blueprint/bugs.json` has the same two-writer shape and does not have this bug, because it is load-modify-save PER EVENT. Both auto-file call sites in dispatch.gleam do `bugs.load` (1635, 1709), then `bugs.append`, then `bugs.save` (1667, 1737) within a few lines -- so the window in which another writer can be clobbered is milliseconds. `blueprint/dag.json` is load-once-PER-RUN: the dispatcher loads the DAG when the run starts and writes it back at every attempt end, so the window is the entire run, minutes to hours.

That is the whole difference between the two boards, and it means the fix needs no design: make the DAG write do what the bug board write already does. Re-read immediately before each write. The DAG is bigger, so a straight re-read-and-overwrite still loses a concurrent edit to the SAME node -- but a captain seeding a NEW node and a dispatcher recording an attempt on an EXISTING one do not collide at all under a re-read, which is exactly the case that lost work here.

--- FIX PLAN 2026-09-09T17:4xZ, Keel, claimed with session ref b58111. Read at HEAD, not from this body ---

ALL FIVE WRITE SITES HAVE ONE SHAPE, so the fix is mechanical rather than a design. `dispatch.gleam` loads once (`:42` for prove-one, `:287` for run) and then, at every write, does `let d = dag.update(<in-memory>, node)` followed by `dag.save(d, path)`: `:141-142` (prove-one claim), `:156-157` (prove-one result), `:614-615` (run claim), `:691-692` (run result), `:763-764` (crash release). Every one writes the WHOLE file from a copy that may be minutes or hours old, and every one is touching exactly ONE node.

That last clause is the whole fix. A writer that changes one node has no reason to write the other 104.

    /// Write `node` into the DAG on disk, re-reading immediately before the
    /// write so a node another writer added since this process loaded
    /// survives. The returned `Dag` is the merged one and the caller adopts
    /// it, so the next write is not based on the stale copy either.
    pub fn save_node(node: Node, path: String) -> Result(Dag, String) {
      use fresh <- result.try(load(path))
      let merged = update(fresh, node)
      use _ <- result.try(save(merged, path))
      Ok(merged)
    }

`dag.update` (`dag.gleam:212`) already replaces one node by id and leaves the rest untouched, so this is three lines and reuses what is there. It is `bugs.gleam`'s load-modify-save, which is why this row's addendum says the fix needs no design.

TWO CONSEQUENCES TO DECIDE RATHER THAN DISCOVER.

1. **Adopting the merged DAG into `RunState.d` changes scheduling.** A node seeded mid-run becomes visible to the running scheduler and can be dispatched by the run that was already up, where today it waits for the next run. That is better, and it is a behaviour change rather than a bug fix, so it should be chosen out loud. Not adopting is also coherent: writes stop clobbering, the run stays blind to new nodes, and the only cost is a seeded node waiting for the next run. RECOMMENDATION: adopt, because a stale in-memory DAG is what this row is about and leaving it stale keeps the defect alive in a quieter form.
2. **A same-node collision is still lost**, and no re-read fixes it: a captain editing a node the dispatcher is also writing loses to whoever writes last. Out of scope and named here so nobody reads the fix as covering it. The case that lost work -- a captain seeding a NEW node while the dispatcher records an attempt on an EXISTING one -- does not collide at all under a per-node write.

THE TEST MUST BE ABLE TO FAIL. Load a fixture DAG, have a second writer append a node to the file on disk, then call the write path and assert the appended node is still there. Run the same test against the current whole-file `dag.save` and confirm it FAILS -- a test that passes both before and after is testing nothing, which is this project's most-repeated defect and the reason this paragraph is in the plan rather than in someone's head.

THE OTHER HALF: DETECTING LOSS THAT ALREADY HAPPENED. The body above says a missing node is indistinguishable from a node never seeded. That is true of `blueprint/dag.json` alone and FALSE of the repository, and the difference is this row's own observation that `Rule30/Statements.lean` has only one writer. A clobbered seed therefore leaves a signature: a `sorry`-ed declaration in `Statements.lean` that no node's `lean_name` names. Run by hand at 17:3xZ against 105 nodes and 107 declarations: ZERO orphans. The two unmatched names are `harness_probe`, which the file documents as deliberately absent from the DAG, and one false positive from a prose line beginning with the word "theorem" inside a doc comment. `harness_probe` is the positive control -- the check finds the one orphan that exists, so its "no" is a result rather than a null check.

That scan is cheap, needs no Lean, and belongs next to the stray-proof section in `status` for the same reason that one does: not going to look IS the failure. It detects PAST loss; `save_node` prevents FUTURE loss; neither substitutes for the other.
bugs.resolution: ccf3580 (Keel), landed on main in 6bbdd25. blueprint/dag.json is now written one node at a time: dag.save_node re-reads the file, replaces by id and returns the merged board, which all six write sites adopt as their new in-memory state (both prove-one sites, all three run sites, reopen). Closure test, and it could fail: run against the old whole-file write the scenario reports the seeded node gone -- 586 announced, 585 passed, 1 failure -- and with save_node, 585 announced and 585 passed. Two things chosen out loud rather than discovered: adopting the merged board lets a node seeded mid-run be dispatched by the run already up, which is a behaviour change and not a bug fix; and a same-node collision is still lost to whoever writes last, which no re-read can fix and was never the case that lost work. writes.gleam's declared-writer registry failed by itself the moment the last dag.save( site disappeared, which is that check working as designed; its risk line now describes per-node writes. The row's claim that a missing node is undetectable is also false and is corrected in the body: Statements.lean has one writer, so a clobbered seed leaves a sorry-ed declaration no node names -- zero orphans over 105 nodes and 107 declarations, with harness_probe as the positive control.

bugs.body:
Every Glob call in this session failed immediately with `ENOENT: no such file or directory, uv_spawn 'rg'` (one variant came back as `EUNKNOWN: unknown error, uv_spawn`). Grep is built on the same binary and would fail identically. Read works fine, so reading a file whose path you already know is unaffected.

This cost me nothing because the brief named `explorer/scratch_rightunbounded_proof.lean` exactly. It would cost a lot on a node where prior work has to be *located* rather than opened: my own notebook records the established P1 habit of globbing `runs/**/<Pascal>.lean` and `explorer/scratch_*.lean` before writing anything, because at least five nodes in this region have closed by retrieval rather than fresh proof. With ripgrep absent that habit is impossible to follow, and the guard correctly denies the Bash fallbacks (`find`, `ls`, `grep`), so there is no way at all to discover a parked file. A worker in that position would re-derive a proof that already exists on disk, or abandon a node that was already closed.

Worth checking whether this is specific to this machine's Claude Code install or something the harness could ship/point at, since the brief-writing side already assumes workers can find parked attempts.

bugs.title: A finding printed below a long table is invisible to a piped reader, because the window shows its rows and cuts its header
bugs.body:
Two instances now, ten hours apart, and the second was measured tonight rather than recalled.

The mechanism: a reader pipes a command through a window chosen BEFORE the command runs -- `| tail -6`, `| head -8`, `| grep 'Open leaves'` -- because they have already decided which part of the output answers their question. The command then answers a different and better question, outside the window. Nothing fails. The value was present, correct, and printed. Distrusting values catches none of this, because the reader never saw the value to distrust.

INSTANCE 1, 2026-09-08, recorded as a clause inside `a-live-sessions-computed-numbers-are-quoted-as-settled`: a profinite figure was re-run through `head -8` and the line was the ninth. That row says, in its own body, "a second and distinct mechanism worth recording separately". It was not recorded separately. This row is that, filed by the same author who wrote the sentence and then did not act on it -- which is itself the third instance of the family, in the notebook rather than the terminal.

INSTANCE 2, 2026-09-09, and it cost an evening. `status` has ended with a "Checked Lean the build cannot see (N)" section since 26fc727 landed at 00:21Z. Between 16:00Z and 17:15Z a captain ran `gleam run -- status` many times, every invocation piped -- `| tail -6`, `| tail -4`, `| grep -iE 'dispatching'`, `| grep 'Open leaves'` -- and then swept the same files by hand, recovering 13 nodes for $10.57 and describing the sweep to its author as work still to be designed. The captain's own account: "the tool answered the question I then spent the night answering by hand, and my reading habit filtered the answer out before it reached me."

THE PRECISE FAILURE IS NOT WHAT EITHER OF US FIRST SAID, and this is the part worth the row. Measured just now against the live checkout:

    $ gleam run -- status | tail -6
      runs/20260908T134658Z/rightDiagonal_antiperiodic_of_odd_driver-1/RightDiagonalAntiperiodicOfOddDriver.lean
      runs/20260908T134658Z/rightDiagonal_driver_flip_iff_white-1/RightDiagonalDriverFlipIffWhite.lean
      runs/20260908T134658Z/rightDiagonal_not_constant-1/RightDiagonalNotConstant.lean
      runs/20260908T205802Z/leftDiagonal_period_le-1/LeftDiagonalPeriodLe.lean
      runs/20260908T224923Z/leftDiagonal_onset_le-3/LeftDiagonalOnsetLe.lean
      runs/20260909T165940Z/leftDiagonal_onset_le-4/LeftDiagonalOnsetLe.lean

The window did NOT exclude the finding. It contained six of the finding's rows and excluded only the header 27 lines above them, which is where all the meaning lives. Six bare paths under `runs/` read as run-directory noise -- exactly what a reader expects to see near the bottom of a status dump and skip. So the defect is not "the reader chose too small a window"; a reader with `tail -6` saw the answer and could not tell it from chaff.

THAT MAKES THIS A LAYOUT BUG WITH A CHEAP FIX, not only a reading-discipline bug. A section whose meaning lives exclusively in its header is invisible to any window that shows its rows. Three candidate fixes, smallest first, none of them yet chosen:

1. Give every row its own marker, so one line out of context still says what it is: `stray: explorer/scratch_rightunbounded_proof.lean` rather than a bare indented path. One line of Gleam, and it survives `tail -1`.
2. Put the count where a habitual window sees it. A digest line at the TOP survives `head`; the section already survives `tail`; nothing survives `grep 'Open leaves'`, and nothing can, which is the honest limit of any layout fix.
3. Non-empty findings could go ABOVE the open-leaf table rather than below it, on the argument that a rare expensive finding outranks the routine listing a captain reads every time. Costs the stability of the output shape.

FALSIFIABILITY, since this row is about a check that could not fail. This row is wrong if a reader piping `tail -6` reliably recognises those six lines. That is testable on a person and has not been tested: n=1 and the person is the one who missed it. What is NOT in doubt is the reproduction above -- the header is outside a 6-line tail window while the rows are inside it, and that is a property of the output, not of the reader.

RELATED: `a-live-sessions-computed-numbers-are-quoted-as-settled` (this mechanism's first instance, as a clause), and `a-check-whose-result-cannot-precede-the-action-is-not-a-check` (same family: there the check could not arrive in time, here the answer arrived and was not read). The family is checks and reports that are structurally incapable of reaching the reader who needs them, and this is its third limb.

--- SHARPENED 2026-09-09T17:3xZ by the filer, after the captain reproduced it and I checked the reproduction against my own command output rather than against the account of it ---

THE SINGLE MOST VALUABLE LINE OF THE FINDING WAS INSIDE THE READER'S OWN WINDOW. One of the six rows in the `tail -6` output above is `runs/20260908T205802Z/leftDiagonal_period_le-1/LeftDiagonalPeriodLe.lean`. That is the exact file the captain "discovered" hours later by an unrelated route -- noticing the word *parked* in a failure summary -- and seeded as `leftDiagonal_period_le_of_black_between`, closed for $0.83. It is also the worked instance of the row this section was built for.

Checked rather than taken: the six-line window above is my own command output, not a report of one. Sorting puts every `explorer/` path before every `runs/` path, so a tail window always lands in the `runs/` rows, and exactly one `runs/` file was added tonight (`runs/20260909T165940Z/leftDiagonal_onset_le-4/LeftDiagonalOnsetLe.lean`, mtime 17:08Z). So `LeftDiagonalPeriodLe.lean` sat third from the end after 17:08Z and SECOND from the end before it -- inside `tail -6` and inside `tail -4`, at every point in the evening, under both windows the captain used.

That closes off the last comfortable reading. Not "the answer was somewhere in the output"; not even "the answer was on screen". The one line that would have saved the evening was on screen, correctly rendered, in a four-line window, repeatedly, and was read as chaff. No amount of distrusting values reaches this, because the value was seen.

THE MECHANISM ATE ITS OWN DESCRIPTION, and this is the strongest instance on the board rather than a lapse beside it. Instance 1 is not merely recorded in another row -- it is recorded in the BODY of a row filed under a different title, about a different defect. That is precisely a finding whose meaning lives where its reader will not be looking, which is this row's own subject. The reason the author did not act on the sentence "worth recording separately" IS the defect the sentence describes. Anyone proposing that the fix is care should start here: the most motivated possible reader, the author, holding the description in his own words, in a file he wrote, did not retrieve it for ten hours.

Which also bounds what a fix can claim. Per-row markers fix the terminal case. Nothing fixes a finding filed inside another finding's body except not doing that: a distinct mechanism gets a distinct row, at the moment it is named, even when the sentence naming it feels like a footnote to the row being written.

bugs.title: The stray-proof section says a file has no holes and never says what it assumes, so a finding and a draft look identical
bugs.body:
`status` separates checked Lean from scratch with one predicate: the file contains no `sorry`. That is the right first cut and it is not the useful one. Of the 31 files the section listed on 2026-09-09, most are theorist scratch for statements that were later seeded properly, and a handful were real theorems -- `explorer/scratch_rightunbounded_proof.lean` held four, including translation equivariance of rule 30, which the board did not have, from a $14.22 session. Nothing distinguishes those two populations at a glance, so the section's reader still has to open 31 files.

`sorry`-free separates a stray from noise. Axioms-within-the-permitted-three separates a finding from a draft, and the harness already knows how to ask: `verify.gleam:48` holds `allowed_axioms`, `:137` parses `#print axioms` output, `:100` judges it.

WHY IT IS NOT A ONE-LINE REUSE. The existing check is node-scoped in three ways a stray file cannot satisfy. It builds `Rule30.Statements` and the node's proof module (`verify_build`, `:71`); it writes a check theorem naming `node.lean_name` on both sides of `type_of%` (`check_source`, `:236`); and it exists to prove the worker proved THE SEEDED STATEMENT, not merely something. A stray file belongs to no node, is not a module in the lake library, and declares whatever names its author chose.

THE SHAPE, and the constraint that picks it. **`status` must not run Lean.** Elaborating 31 Mathlib-importing files is tens of minutes and takes the build lock a live run is queueing on, and a `status` that blocks for minutes is a `status` nobody runs -- which would reproduce `a-reader-s-pre-chosen-output-window-hides-a-finding-whose-meaning-is-in-its-header` for a third time inside the same section. A `sweep` verb fails for the reason the section is in `status` at all: not going to look IS the failure.

So: check when the lock is already held and free, cache the verdict, print the cached verdict.

1. **Per-row marker, first and independently.** Each row prints `stray: <path>` rather than a bare indented path, so one line out of context still says what it is. One line of Gleam; closes the tail-window half of the reading bug; needs none of the rest.
2. **Cache keyed by content hash**, one entry per stray file: hash, verdict, when. A file whose hash is absent prints `unchecked`, which is inert and correct rather than silently missing -- the stale-value rule. Content hash rather than mtime because a checkout, a rebase or a worktree moves mtimes and nothing else.
3. **Sweep at the end of a run**, when the dispatcher already owns the lock and no attempt is queued behind it: elaborate each unchecked stray, cap the number per run so a run's tail stays bounded, oldest first. A run killed before the sweep leaves entries `unchecked`, which is the inert failure and not a wrong answer.
4. **Elaborate a COPY, never the file.** Write `harness/build/strays/<hash>.lean`: the stray's source, then one `#print axioms <name>` per top-level `theorem`/`lemma` name parsed from it. Run `lake env lean` once over the copy and reuse `parse_axioms`/`allowed_axioms` verbatim. This is the same trick `verify_check` (`:88`) already uses for the check theorem, and it means a stray file is never written to by the harness.

WHAT AN "AXIOMS OK" VERDICT WOULD AND WOULD NOT MEAN, because this is the seam that will mislead someone. It means the file elaborates and its theorems rest only on `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound` -- a real theorem, not a draft. It does NOT mean the file closes anything. A stray can be perfectly proved and prove a statement no node wants, or a weaker one that looks like the node's; the whole reason `check_source` puts `type_of%` against the seeded statement is that a proof of something NEAR the target is the failure mode a proof checker cannot see. So the verdict promotes a file from "worth opening" to "worth reading", and never to "seed this". Anyone who reads it as the latter has re-invented the bug `type_of%` exists to stop.

Filed rather than left in the closed row's suggested-fix clause and in two peer messages, which is where this design was living an hour ago. That is exactly the shape `a-reader-s-pre-chosen-output-window-...` says is invisible: a distinct piece of work described inside a different row's body. Related: that row, and `an-abandoned-attempts-parked-proof-is-invisible-to-everything-downstream` (fixed, `26fc727`), whose section this extends.

--- CORRECTED 2026-09-09T18:2xZ by the filer, before building: the cost estimate above was wrong by an order of magnitude. I wrote "tens of minutes" for the population and measured it instead: 2.5s, 5.3s, 5.8s, 9.0s and 19.7s for five files with warm oleans, so 31 files is two to four minutes and each new one is seconds. The design does not change -- a status that blocks for even two minutes on the lock a live run queues on is still a status nobody runs -- but the argument for it now rests on a measurement rather than on a number I made up, and the difference matters because the wrong number would also have justified designs this one does not.
bugs.resolution: 8d2debf and ff10ea4 (Keel), landed on main in daac3ad. New harness/stray.gleam elaborates each stray and asks what its theorems depend on, against verify.allowed_axioms (now one public definition rather than two copies). Verdicts: clean / assumes / broken / no theorems, cached by content hash under harness/build/, swept at the end of a run where the lake lock is already held, capped at twelve files. status prints the cached verdict and never runs Lean, because a status that blocks for minutes is a status nobody runs -- which is how this section went unread for an evening. Every row also names itself now (stray: proves X  <path>), which is the layout half of a-reader-s-pre-chosen-output-window-...: verified in the live checkout, gleam run -- status | tail -6 prints six rows that each say what they are. Closure test, and it can fail: 601 announced, 601 passed, four tests running real lake env lean against test/fixture-project, one of which must come back dirty via a declared axiom in a file with no sorry in it -- exactly the file the sorry filter alone would have called a finding. My tens-of-minutes estimate in the body was wrong by an order of magnitude and is corrected there: measured 2.5s, 5.3s, 5.8s, 9.0s and 19.7s. Three defects were caught by the machinery rather than by me and are named in 8d2debf: writes.gleam flagged the new module's raw writes on day one, the suite fell to 325 of an announced 597 when the sweep ran inside test runs, and the fixture tests caught first_error matching a string this toolchain never prints (Lean 4.33 writes error(lean.unknownIdentifier):), which had made a broken file's verdict 120 characters of absolute path and no error at all. All 36 rows read unchecked until the next run ends and fills the cache.
