bugs.title: An attempt filed as budget_exhausted had already written a complete, sorry-free proof of its own node
bugs.body:
Worked instance, 2026-09-09T17:45Z, run 20260909T174534Z. `centerColumn_run_boundary` was dispatched to Cadence on sonnet with a $4.00 ceiling. The attempt ended `budget_exhausted` at **$0.81** -- a fifth of the ceiling -- and the node stayed open. The parked file `runs/20260909T174534Z/centerColumn_run_boundary-1/CenterColumnRunBoundary.lean` contains `theorem centerColumn_run_boundary` with **zero `sorry`**. The proof was finished. The harness recorded a failure and moved the finished proof to a directory nothing reads.

This is the same underlying defect as `a-cli-success-result-with-no-report-is-filed-as-budget-exhausted` -- a CLI result with no structured report is filed under a budget outcome -- and this row is not a duplicate of it but a record of what that defect COSTS. The prior row says the outcome name is wrong and the attempt counts against the ladder. This one says the work was complete and was discarded. Those are different harms and the second is the expensive one: an outcome of `budget_exhausted` at a fifth of the ceiling is a visible anomaly a captain could notice, but nothing anywhere says the proof is done.

Why it matters more now than it did: the stray-proof sweep in `status` lists this file, so it is no longer invisible. But the sweep's verdict is `sorry`-free and nothing more, so the file reads as ordinary scratch beside a theorist's drafts. The open row `stray-lean-is-separated-from-scratch-by-sorry-alone-and-never-by-what-it-assumes` proposes an axiom check, and that would promote this file from 'worth opening' to 'worth reading' -- but it would still not say 'this closes the node it is named after', which is the fact that actually matters here and which `type_of%` already knows how to decide.

Suggested fix, and it is small because the machinery exists: when an attempt ends without a report but its proof file is present, run the existing verification -- the `type_of%` check theorem and `#print axioms` -- against the parked file before filing the outcome. If it passes, the node is proved and the outcome is `proved`; if it fails, file the budget outcome as now. The verifier is already written and already runs on this exact input in the success path. Nothing new has to be decided; the check simply has to be reached on a path that currently skips it.

EVIDENCE AND THREE CORRECTIONS, added by Fathom 2026-09-10T14:45Z from session rule30-5d, before any fix was designed. The central premise HOLDS and is now checked rather than inferred: verify.check_source inlined against the parked file -- `theorem harness_check : type_of% @Statements.centerColumn_run_boundary := @centerColumn_run_boundary` -- gives `lake env lean` exit 0 and `'harness_check' depends on axioms: [propext, Quot.sound]`, the same axioms Vesper's landed proof reported. The seeded statement at HEAD is character-identical to the parked theorem's and has not been touched at that name since. A complete, clean-axiom proof of the node was filed as a failure.

Three things in the body above are wrong, and the third matters for the fix.
(1) Cadence was on HAIKU, not sonnet. Vesper was the sonnet attempt, and Vesper is the one that proved it.
(2) The node did not stay open. Vesper closed it 46 seconds later at 17:53:36Z for a second $0.81; dag.json has it `proved`. The cost is a duplicated attempt, not an open node.
(3) 'budget_exhausted at $0.81, a fifth of the $4.00 ceiling' frames a DOLLAR budget, and this was the ROUND budget. summary.txt says so: 'the worker stopped reporting, and the harness's round budget ran out asking it to'. events.jsonl shows five 150-byte nudges at 17:50:49, :59, 17:51:14, :32, :52, then the give-up. So 'a fifth of the ceiling' is not a detectable anomaly for this class -- a round-budget ending can land at any spend.

ROOT CAUSE, which no row on this board states. The worker never called StructuredOutput: zero tool_use by that name across all 316 events, and all five `result` events are subtype=success, stop_reason=end_turn, structured_output=false. Its prose under the nudges reads, verbatim: "I've already called StructuredOutput at the end of my previous response to provide the structured report for this proof attempt. The proof of `centerColumn_run_boundary` is complete and verified to build successfully." It said a variant of that five times. The nudge loop was arguing with a confidently-wrong worker, which no number of nudges wins -- and the worker's claim about the PROOF was true; it was wrong only about having reported.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE FIX. It supports the suggested fix and moves it earlier. If the parked file is verified at the FIRST report-less turn where a proof file exists, the five nudges never happen either: the node closes at 17:50:49 instead of being nudged to death and re-proved by a second persona. Nudging is only worth spending on when there is no verifiable proof file sitting there.

SCOPE OF THE COUNTS, and the sharper statement of the decoder bug. Added by Fathom 2026-09-10T15:4x, after Rowan reproduced the scan independently and got a different total. Both totals were right and one scope was unstated -- mine. Measured over the ATTEMPT logs, `runs/*/*/events.jsonl`: 166 files, 774 rate-limit events, statuses 651 allowed / 117 allowed_warning / 6 rejected. Over the RUN-ROOT logs, `runs/*/events.jsonl`: 85 files, 29 events, 22 allowed / 7 allowed_warning / 0 rejected, and no integer utilizations at all. Both together: 251 files, 803 events, 673 / 124 / 6. All six integer-valued five-hour utilizations are in the attempt logs, so the finding is scope-independent; the number simply should not have been able to travel without its glob.

The six, in full:
  u=0 allowed          x4  (harmless)
  u=0 allowed_warning  x1  (harmless)
  u=1 rejected         x1  runs/20260907T210826Z/column_settledConfig_eq-1

THE BUG STATED AT THE RANGE RATHER THAN AT THE INSTANCE, which is Rowan's framing and is better than "a full window sends 1". JSON serialises exactly two utilization values without a decimal point, `0` and `1`, because every value in between carries one. So `decode.float` was blind at BOTH ENDS of the range and nowhere else -- blind five times at the empty end where blindness cost nothing, and once at the full end, which is the only reading that must park a run. That is why any ordinary sample of this field makes the decoder look perfect, and why five harmless instances sat in the record as company for the expensive one.

The `allowed_warning` zero is kept separate from the four `allowed` zeros deliberately rather than tidied in with them: it is harmless only because `hit_ceiling` tests the `allowed` PREFIX. If that test ever narrows to an exact match, that row stops being harmless, and a reader who had been told "the zeros are all allowed" would not know to go looking.
bugs.resolution: 62a3ddf (Fathom): premise confirmed by running the harness's own check by hand on the parked file (type_of% @Statements.centerColumn_run_boundary, lake env lean exit 0, axioms [propext, Quot.sound] — the same axioms the later landed proof reported). Root cause was in no row: the worker never called StructuredOutput (zero tool_use by that name across 316 events; all five result events subtype=success, stop_reason=end_turn, structured_output=false) and told the nudge loop five times that it had, while being CORRECT about the proof. Nudging cannot distinguish 'no work' from 'work done, not described'; the file can. FIXED IN THE WRONG PLACE FIRST, and that is the part worth keeping: I built the pickup as a mitigation for the naming bug so I wired it into act_on, the path where the naming was wrong. Rowan's instance an hour later (runs/20260910T151819Z/periodicFrom_trans_period-1, turn-ceiling ending, parked file proves the node, second dispatch re-derived it for $0.88) had a CORRECT name and walked straight past it. Every instance I had carried both bugs at once, so the misplacement was invisible — a sampling error, not a coding one. It is now a salvage step on the Role, applied once in drive to any ending that is not already Finished, so an ending nobody has imagined gets the check for free. Includes Abandoned, on Rowan's argument that the project's founding rule (nobody declares a proof done by assertion; lake decides) has only ever been enforced in one direction. The bar is the verifier and never the presence of a file, and the negative test pins it. A lost build lock is distinguished from a failed proof via Deps.undecided (Keel's catch: the run's verifier returns BuildFailed(lock_held_message) on a lost lock, which correlates with load, so my check would have discarded finished proofs exactly when the machine was busiest). A salvaged close suppresses the estimate but keeps the report — the suite caught me dropping the worker's filed bugs and proposed lemmas with it — and is visible in dag.json, summary.txt and the run summary row. Suite 649/649, exit 0.

bugs.title: Nothing stops a new Lean-running call being wired straight into the dispatcher, and the suite goes slow rather than red
bugs.body:
Three times in one evening, one agent wired a new Lean-running call directly into `dispatch.gleam` instead of through `Env`, and each time the suite -- not review -- was what said so. The `Env` fields for `verifier`, `check_proposals` and `sweep_strays` each carry a doc comment saying, in different words, "injected because the real one runs Lean and a test must be able to avoid it". All three were read past.

WHAT IT COSTS, and it is not the fix. Each trip cost one suite run to notice and one small edit to fix. The expensive part is the SHAPE of the failure: a test suite that runs real Lean does not fail, it gets slow, and a slow suite with no failing assertion is the hardest thing in this repo to diagnose. Measured 2026-09-09: wiring the statement gate directly took the suite from 48 seconds to past ten minutes without a single failed assertion, and the run that did report failures (325 passed, 3 failures against an announced 607) reported them because modules were CANCELLED, not because anything was wrong with the code under test. A reader who trusts the pass count learns nothing; a reader who reads the denominator learns only that something was cancelled.

WHY A COMMENT CANNOT FIX IT. The three comments are good comments. They are placed where the field is DEFINED, and the mistake is made where a new call is WRITTEN -- a different file region, often a different session, always by someone who has not just read the type. A rule that is only discoverable after you have broken it is not a rule, it is a post-mortem. Note that the same agent read all three comments during the same evening while making the mistake all three times.

THE FIX THIS PROJECT ALREADY OWNS, one file over. `writes.gleam` solves exactly this shape for a different resource: it scans `harness/src` at test time and reports raw `simplifile` writes sitting in a module that is not a declared writer implementation, "which is what a new one looks like on its first day". That check caught the new `stray.gleam` on its first day, and caught `blueprint/dag.json` losing its last declared writer during an unrelated rename. It works because it is derived at run time from the source rather than remembered by a person.

The same scan applied to a second resource: which modules may invoke `lake`. Declare the implementations -- `verify.gleam`, `seed.gleam`, `stray.gleam`, `lean_fixture.gleam` -- and report any `shell.run(` whose arguments mention `lake` or `lean` in a module outside that set. `dispatch.gleam` would then fail the suite the moment a Lean call is written into it directly, naming the file and line, instead of the suite silently taking twenty times as long. Cheap, and its author does not have to know it exists.

WHAT WOULD ALSO WORK, and is more invasive: make the live implementations unavailable to a test by construction rather than by convention -- a separate module the test build does not link, or a `Deps`-style record threaded through the dispatch path so a direct call has nothing to call. Both are real designs and both are larger than the scan.

NOT filed as a complaint about the three comments. Filed because a fourth session will make the same trip, and because the countermeasure already exists in this codebase and is proven -- it caught two real defects tonight in changes that had nothing to do with what it was written for.

bugs.title: No verb re-verifies a proved node, so changing a statement strands its Checked type block with the old signature
bugs.body:
The Checked type block in a proof file is described in CLAUDE.md as the only sentence in the file the harness stands behind: the harness writes it after lake build and the type_of% check pass. Nothing can rewrite it afterwards. `seed check` only adjudicates proposals, and there is no verb that re-runs verification against an already-proved node.

So a captain who changes a seeded statement leaves every affected proof file asserting, in the harness's own voice, a signature that is no longer the statement. Instance: the 2026-09-09 stepMod retrofit (a64f256) changed six statements; four carried a Checked type block and all four went stale at once. Nothing in the build notices, because the block is a comment.

This is the well-formed-and-wrong family in its purest form. The block is confident, correctly formatted, attributed to the component with the most authority in the repo, and wrong. A reader checking whether a proof matches its statement will read it and stop there.

WORKED AROUND, NOT FIXED, at a64f256: I refreshed the four by hand from what #check printed against Rule30.Statements, and rewrote the parenthetical to say a captain refreshed them during the retrofit rather than claiming a verification run that did not happen. That preserves the block's provenance claim, which is the only property that made it worth having, but it is a captain's word where the point was that it was not.

WHAT WOULD FIX IT: a verb that re-runs the existing type_of% check against a node already marked proved and rewrites the block from the result. The machinery exists in verify.gleam; what is missing is an entry point that does not require dispatching an attempt.

SECOND, SMALLER FINDING: Rule30/Proofs/LeftDiagonalOnsetLeOfStepModPreperiod.lean carries no Checked type block at all, so the invariant that a closed node's file has one does not hold today. Worth deciding whether that is a bug or an accepted gap before the verb above is written, since the verb has to do something about it.

--- AMENDED 2026-09-10 by Keel (premise pass before any fix; commands in agents/Keel.md) ---

THE SECOND FINDING IS TWO FILES, NOT ONE, AND THE 36 SPLITS. Measured over the 113 nodes marked proved in blueprint/dag.json, mapped to paths with dag.proof_path's own pascal_case rather than a reimplementation of it: 113 proved, 113 files, one-to-one, no parked strays. 77 carry a Checked type block and 36 do not. That 36 is two different things:

  34 files were born BEFORE 5ee56fc (2026-09-06 21:43, where the annotation landed). No file born before it carries a block. This is a historical cohort, not drift, and MUST NEVER BE REPORTED AS DRIFT — a verb that flags all 34 on its first run turns its own output into noise, which is how a check stops being read. They want a distinct word (unannotated, not drifted). Whether to backfill them is open and goes to Rowan as its own proposal.

  2 files are live violations, and they are a DEFECT, NOT A GAP:
    leftDiagonal_onset_le_of_line              (2026-09-08)
    leftDiagonal_onset_le_of_stepMod_preperiod (2026-09-09, the one this row named)

THE CAUSE, REPRODUCED. Both attempts verified and then annotate failed identically. From each attempt's events.jsonl:
  verify   ... "verified": true, "verdict": "VERIFIED. Axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound"
  annotate ... "statement": "", "written": false, "reason": "no statement to write: the check output had no #check line"
Generating exactly what verify.check_source emits for leftDiagonal_onset_le_of_line and running lake env lean on it gives:

  Statements.leftDiagonal_onset_le_of_line
    (h :
      forall (m : N), leftDiagonal (m + 1) (m + 2) = true or ...
    (k : N) : exists p > 0, exists N <= k, PeriodicFrom (leftDiagonal k) p N

The NAME IS ALONE ON ITS LINE: Lean wrapped the signature because the binders are long. verify.statement_of matches only starts_with(name <> " ") or name <> ":", so it matches nothing and returns "". These two are the only proved statements whose binders wrap the head, which is exactly why it is these two and no others.

So the parser succeeds on every statement except the ones with the most binders, and the failure is silent in both directions: the attempt still reports VERIFIED, the node still closes correctly, and the file simply has no block. Every reader downstream then reads a missing block as an accepted gap. The annotate event was accurate and the conclusion drawn from it was false.

THE FIX to statement_of is to also accept the name as the ENTIRE line. That cannot reintroduce the hazard the space-or-colon rule guards (a statement whose name extends another's), because Statements.foo alone on a line is distinguishable from Statements.foo_bar alone on a line by the same equality.

WHAT THE VERB DOES ABOUT THE 2: re-runs the real check and writes the block from that result. That is not synthesis — it is the verification that should have happened on 2026-09-08 finally happening. It must not fabricate a block for a file it did not just verify.

CONSTRAINT ON THE VERB (Rowan): whatever it calls verified must mean elaborates against the seeded statement with only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound — not merely elaborates.

STILL OPEN AT AMENDMENT TIME: whether any of the 77 existing blocks disagrees with Rule30/Statements.lean at HEAD. A textual comparison cannot answer it, because the block is Lean's PRINTED signature rather than the source text; the honest answer needs all 77 elaborated, which is the verb itself. Deferred while a run was in flight. Not answered is not the same as zero.
bugs.resolution: 8611130 and f19a39d (Keel): `reverify <node-id>` re-runs the real check against an already-proved node and rewrites its Checked type block; `reverify --all` surveys every proved node and writes nothing, so the files predating the annotation are reported as unannotated rather than backfilled in one unreviewable commit. Root cause of the row's second finding fixed too: verify.statement_of matched only `name <> " "` or `name <> ":"`, and Lean puts the name alone on its line when the binders wrap, so it returned "" for exactly the statements with the most binders and annotate wrote no block. Both affected files repaired by running the verb. CLOSURE TEST: `gleam run -- reverify --all` over all 116 proved nodes reports zero DRIFTED, zero FAILED, zero NO SIGNATURE; 82 blocks agree with Rule30/Statements.lean, 34 files predate the annotation. So no block on main asserts a type that is not the statement. The sweep also found two defects in itself: annotation_in and annotated each split on the full heading rather than the '**Checked type**' marker, so five hand-refreshed blocks read as absent and would have been DUPLICATED rather than replaced; fixed at f19a39d with four tests. Suite 629/629, exit 0.

bugs.title: Addressing a peer by identity name reaches a stale offline Remote Control session, not the live local one
bugs.body:
Filed by Fathom on 2026-09-10 at 14:31Z, after doing it, from session rule30-5d [0a2b6a]. Two instances inside one minute, one each way, between two sessions that had both just run /startup.

WHAT HAPPENED. /startup Job 1 says the point of agents/sessions.json is that a peer can reach you by identity rather than by guessing, and that once the title hook applies a peer can SendMessage Keel instead of rule30-57. I sent to the bare name Keel. It resolved, with success:true and no warning, to Keel [2a32f0] — a Remote Control row last active 13h earlier, offline — and the message was queued for delivery whenever that machine reconnects. The live Keel was rule30-93 [1e45cf], started 90 seconds earlier and busy. Keel independently hit the same thing addressing me and fell back to rule30-5d; each of us reported it to the other as a surprise.

WHY IT RESOLVES WRONG. The title hook that turns a ListAgents row's name into the identity fires on Dib's next prompt, not on the sessions.json commit, so for the first minutes of every session the live row is still named rule30-XX while dead Remote Control rows already carry the identity name. During that window the identity name matches exactly one agent -- the stale one -- so the send does not disambiguate and does not warn. Sending to the same name a minute later, after the repaint, would have worked. By contrast SendMessage Rowan did error with '2 agents are named Rowan', because there the live row had already repainted and two rows collided; the failure is specifically the case where only the dead row carries the name.

WHY IT MATTERS. The delivery is not dropped, it is deferred: an instruction written for a peer working right now arrives at an unrelated session hours later, with the context that made it correct long gone. That is the shape of the misaddressed-briefing failure in the Boundaries section of CLAUDE.md, reached this time by obeying the startup skill rather than by carelessness. It bites hardest in exactly the window /startup runs in, when a session has just learned peer identities and has not yet learned that they are not yet addresses.

CLOSURE TEST. /startup Job 3 tells the reader to address a peer by the name-and-ref exactly as the ListAgents row prints it for as long as that row still reads rule30-XX, and says why: the identity name is not an address until the title hook repaints, and an offline Remote Control row may hold that name in the meantime. It also says a bare-name send that succeeds is not evidence it reached the live peer -- check the tool result's description of the recipient, which does say 'offline right now -- delivery is queued'.

bugs.title: The route checker adds two spaces to the first tactic line, so a pre-indented route is reported as not closing
bugs.body:
Filed by Rowan on 2026-09-10 from session rule30-38 [d5696e], reproduced byte-exact rather than inferred. `seed.check_source` (harness/src/harness/seed.gleam:206) builds the route check file as `imports <> "
" <> declaration <> "
  " <> route.tactics <> "
"`. That `"
  "` prepends two spaces to the FIRST tactic line only. A route whose tactics are already indented -- which is how every route in blueprint/proposals/next.json is written, and the natural way to write one -- therefore lands with its first tactic at column 4 and every following line at column 2. Lean sets a tactic block's indentation from its first tactic, so every subsequent line falls OUTSIDE the block: the block contains one tactic, and Lean reports `unsolved goals` at the `by`.

CONSEQUENCE, and it is the reason this is `blocks` rather than `friction`: the route checker is the adjudicator a captain uses to decide whether a proposed node is landable, and it produces FALSE NEGATIVES. On last night's seeder proposal (runs/20260909T230801Z, six P1 nodes) it reported three of the four claimed routes as DOES NOT CLOSE. All four close. I elaborated each one with the harness's own imports and the proposal's own statement, differing from check_source only in dropping the two spaces: four files, `lake env lean`, exit 0 on all four.

REPRODUCTION, periodicFrom_trans_period. Harness way -> `4:80: error: unsolved goals` with goal state showing `n` and `hn` introduced and nothing else done, which is exactly `intro n hn` (the first tactic) having run alone. Fixed way -> exit 0. The `4:80` matches the position `gleam run -- seed check` itself reported, character for character, so this is the same failure and not a lookalike.

WHY IT WAS NOT CAUGHT, and this is the part worth keeping. It does not fail uniformly. `leftDiagonal_not_both_eventually_white` passes the broken checker, because its first tactic is `induction k with` and Lean's induction-alternative parser tolerates the `| zero =>` lines at column 2. So the checker returns a MIXTURE of closes and does-not-close on a set of routes that all close, and a mixture reads as discrimination -- it looks exactly like a checker doing its job. A checker that failed everything would have been found in an hour.

The seeder's own scratch, explorer/seed_scratch_routes.lean, holds three of these routes with correct indentation and elaborates exit 0. So the record already contained the contradiction: seeder says compiles, `seed check` says unsolved goals, and the stray sweep in `status` reports that same file as `unchecked`. Three records, three answers, and the one with a mechanism behind it was the seeder's.

SUGGESTED FIX: join with `"
"` and let the route carry its own indentation, or normalise the route's indentation before joining -- but not both, or an unindented route breaks instead. Whichever is chosen, the test has to cover a MULTI-LINE route whose tactics are pre-indented; a single-line route cannot exhibit this and a route starting with `induction ... with` masks it. `witness_source` at seed.gleam:511 is NOT affected: it emits `#eval` and has no tactic block.
bugs.resolution: 37e58ce, landed at b95bd06 (Keel): seed.check_source joined declaration to route with '\n  ', prepending two spaces to raw tactic text. A route is naturally written already indented under its `by`, so the FIRST line landed at column 4 and every later line at column 2; Lean opens a tactic block at the first tactic's column, so the rest of the route fell outside it and elaboration reported 'unsolved goals' — indistinguishable from a genuinely open node, which is why this was blocks and not a papercut. `indented` now replaces the COMMON left margin with exactly two spaces, so relative depth inside the block (what Lean reads to nest cases arms) survives byte for byte; blank lines are excluded from the margin measurement, since counting them finds a margin of zero and over-indents every real line. CLOSURE TEST, end to end rather than unit: `gleam run -- seed check` over blueprint/proposals/next.json in the shared checkout reported 'closes the statement' for leftDiagonal_periodicFrom_of_rowNat_agree, rowNat_agree_forward and rowNat_testBit_zero — all three of which were reported DOES NOT CLOSE before the fix. The fourth, leftDiagonal_onset_le_not_of_black_ladder, was correctly refused as WRONG OBJECT because the landed statement is the pointwise form while the proposal holds the seeder's forall form; that is a-verified-route-can-be-verified-against-the-wrong-object firing as designed, and it independently confirms that guard still works through the changed code path. Its route elaborated with the three permitted axioms in explorer/rowan_routecheck/ before the landing, so four for four in substance. Suite 653/653, exit 0. Evidence gathered by Rowan.

bugs.title: A per-test timeout in a Lean-invoking test aborts the whole run_test module, so 289 tests never run and the pass line still reads fine
bugs.body:
Found by Fathom on 2026-09-10, from a run captured unfiltered after Keel hit the same numbers and could not name them. Two sessions, two worktrees, two branches, identical result: announced 617/609, `325 passed, 3 failures`, exit 1.

WHAT HAPPENS. `prove_one_writes_its_record_in_an_attempt_directory_test` (test/run_test.gleam:500) runs the real `prove_one`, which shells out to Lean on the way: harness_ffi:collect/3 <- harness@shell.run (src/harness/shell.gleam:62) <- harness@verify.statement_resolves (src/harness/verify.gleam:319) <- harness@dispatch.statement_gate (src/harness/dispatch.gleam:1243) <- dispatch.prove_one. eunit killed that test for exceeding a PER-TEST timeout -- `Reason(Timeout(...))` with the stack above, not the harness's own `shell.run` budget, which returns `Error("timeout after N ms")` and would surface as an ordinary failed assertion.

THE DEFECT IS NOT THE TIMEOUT, IT IS WHAT THE TIMEOUT COSTS. One test being killed did not cost one test. eunit aborted the entire `run_test` module -- the other two reported failures are its bookkeeping for the first, `Reason(Undefined), Desc("module 'run_test'")` and `Reason(Blame([19,4]))` -- and 289 of 617 tests never ran. So `3 failures` is one failure, and the 289 are invisible: nothing in `325 passed, 3 failures` says that half the suite was never reached.

WHY THE COUNT IS ALWAYS 325. This is the part that defeated two people for an afternoon. The cause is load-sensitive -- a cold `harness/test/fixture-project/.lake`, a second suite, a live prover, anything that makes Lean slow enough -- but the CONSEQUENCE is deterministic, because module order and the abort point do not vary. So the shortfall appears and disappears with machine load while always producing the same pass count, which reads like a fixed bug rather than a timing one and sends you looking in the wrong place. Keel and Fathom independently produced `325 passed, 3 failures` on different branches in different worktrees.

WHAT IT COST ALREADY, on 2026-09-10 alone: one session read `325 passed, 3 failures` as a healthy run of a suite it believed had 609 tests and attributed 2 of the 3 failures to its own new tests -- which, if the shape was this one, had never run at all. A second session lost forty minutes reading an empty output file as a slow compile. The suite's own `suite_size` announcement is the only thing that catches any of it, and it catches it only if the reader compares the two numbers by hand every single time.

RELATED, NOT DUPLICATE. `gleam-test-can-fail-to-boot-and-it-does-not-look-like-a-test-failure` is the suite dying BEFORE it starts. This is the suite starting, running a third of itself, silently dropping the rest, and exiting with a pass line.

NOT VERIFIED, and it is the first thing to check: eunit's default per-test timeout is believed to be 5 seconds, but nothing has been found in this project that sets or inherits it, and no one has confirmed the value. That belief is the obvious explanation and is exactly the kind of plausible unchecked premise this board exists to catch -- check it before designing on it.

CLOSURE TEST. A `gleam test` whose Lean-invoking test times out reports that test as ONE failure and still runs the rest of `run_test`, so passed + failures + skipped equals the announced total; and a test asserts that a deliberately slow shell call inside a test fails that test alone rather than ending its module. The stronger fix, if it is available, is that the Lean-invoking tests carry an explicit per-test timeout sized for a cold fixture rather than inheriting a default sized for a pure-Erlang unit test.

THE TIMEOUT IS 50 SECONDS, NOT 5, AND THAT MAKES THIS WORSE. Found by Keel on 2026-09-10 from the artifact rather than from recall: gleeunit sets its own eunit options in build/packages/gleeunit/src/gleeunit.erl:55 -- `Options = [verbose, no_tty, {report, {gleeunit_progress, [{colored, true}]}}, {scale_timeouts, 10}]`. eunit's default per-test timeout is 5 seconds and `scale_timeouts` multiplies it, so every test in this suite is already allowed 50. Nothing in this project sets its own; gleam.toml, src and test carry only the harness's own shell budgets.

This retires the NOT VERIFIED paragraph above, and it inverts the obvious fix. At 5 seconds, "a test that shells out to Lean sometimes overruns" is unremarkable and raising the limit is the natural response. At 50 it is not a tight limit at all: it means whatever tripped it was astonishingly slow, on a suite whose healthy full run is under a minute. Raising the parameter would mean reaching for 100 or 200 seconds, which is not a fix but a wider window to be slow in. It also rules out a class of explanation -- this is not a test sitting near a boundary and tipping over. Something took more than fifty seconds inside `statement_resolves`, and a cold `harness/test/fixture-project/.lake` being built underneath it is exactly the kind of thing that does.

So the framing survives and sharpens: the abort is the defect and the timeout is a parameter, and the parameter turns out to be generous rather than stingy, which means fixing the parameter is not fixing anything.

TWO MORE THINGS FOR WHOEVER TAKES THIS, both Keel's. Keel's run 1 compiled BEFORE the statement_of fix landed, so had verify_test run at all its two new tests could not have passed -- they would have been named as failures, and were not. That closes "the aborted module took them with it" without needing any comparison between the two sessions' runs. And the deeper suspicion, which is about the test rather than the timeout: `dispatch.Env` exists precisely so that tests do not run Lean, and a test reaching the real `statement_resolves` through the real `prove_one` looks like one that slipped that pattern. If that is right this row has two fixes at different depths -- stop the abort, and stop the test needing Lean at all -- and only the first one helps every other Lean-invoking test.

bugs.title: A command that mutates as it walks reports where it stopped, not what it already did
bugs.body:
`git worktree remove --force <dir>` printed `error: failed to delete '<dir>': Permission denied` and exited non-zero. That message is TRUE about the outcome and SILENT about the side effects: the command deletes as it walks, so it had already removed an unknown number of files before it reached the one a running build held open. Reading a non-zero exit as "the operation did not happen" is the natural reading and it is wrong.

WHY IT IS ITS OWN SHAPE, distinct from the two other failure kinds this project has named today. A check that fails silently gives you no answer. A classifier with a default gives you an invented answer. THIS gives you a true answer to a question you did not ask — it reports the terminating condition, and the reader wants the extent of the mutation. Nothing about reading the message more carefully helps, because the information is not in it.

WHAT IT COST: a causal claim built on the assumption of no-op, asserted to a peer, retracted, and then re-asserted in the opposite direction. It reached a third party as a settled fact inside minutes. The truth remains unknown (see `an-orphaned-lake-build-outlives-the-suite-that-spawned-it`).

THE GENERAL QUESTION THIS ROW ASKS, which is worth more than the git instance: which commands in this harness mutate before they can fail, and does anything downstream treat a failed command as a no-op? Candidates to audit: partial file writes, `dag.save` / `bugs` board rewrites, an interrupted `lake build` leaving a half-populated `.lake`, and any `simplifile` sequence with more than one write in it. A retry-on-failure path is the dangerous consumer, because it assumes the failed attempt left nothing behind.

NOT A FIX ON ITS OWN: catching the error and reporting it better does not help either, since the harness cannot know the extent of a partial deletion any more than the reader can. What helps is either making the mutation atomic (write-then-rename) or making the failure path state explicitly that the target is now in an unknown state.

bugs.title: An aborted suite leaves a from-scratch Mathlib build running with no parent, and nobody knows if it stops
bugs.body:
When `run_test`'s prove_one test is killed by the eunit timeout, the `lake build Rule30.Statements` it shelled through `verify.statement_resolves` is NOT reaped. On 2026-09-10 one was observed still running with its parent erl dead: 24 `lean` processes, 2 `lake`, building Mathlib from scratch into a throwaway worktree.

ESTABLISHED:
- Spawned by `statement_resolves`; building Mathlib into the cold worktree, not into anything shared.
- Outlived its parent erl by at least six minutes. Parent PID confirmed dead.
- Wrote NEITHER the live checkout's `.lake` NOR `harness/test/fixture-project/.lake` — independently measured, zero files modified in both across ~11:13-11:17. The shared tree was never at risk.
- Gone by ~11:16; a sweep at that moment reaped nothing.

WHAT ENDED IT IS UNKNOWN, and this row exists partly to stop that gap being filled with a guess. Two candidates: a `git worktree remove --force` that had failed with `Permission denied` minutes earlier (which deletes as it walks — see `a-failed-destructive-command-is-read-as-a-no-op-but-mutates-as-it-walks`), or the build ending for its own reasons. NO EVIDENCE SEPARATES THEM. A directory mtime that looked like it did cannot: a directory's mtime moves on deletion as readily as on creation, so it is consistent with both.

Both causal stories were asserted confidently, by two different sessions, in opposite directions, within twenty minutes, each built on the previous one's artifact. Neither is in this row as a finding.

WHETHER THESE SELF-TERMINATE IS UNRESOLVED, and it decides the fix. If they do, an aborted cold suite is merely wasteful. If they do not, every framework agent who runs a suite in a fresh worktree and walks away leaves an hours-long Mathlib build running unowned. Those want different responses, and the comfortable answer — that they stop on their own — is the dangerous one to assume, because it makes the defect look bounded and nobody then builds the reaping.

THE EXPERIMENT, UNRUN, AND WHY: start a suite in a cold worktree, let it abort, touch nothing, and watch. It costs a from-scratch Mathlib build and was not worth the machine on the day. Recorded here rather than dropped so it stays available if the cost ever falls.

UPSTREAM: this only happens because `prove_one` shells real Lean at a repo_root with no `.lake`. Fixing that removes the orphan along with the abort.

bugs.title: Three sessions rediscovered an open row in one afternoon because nothing searches the board by what you have in hand
bugs.body:
On 2026-09-10, three sessions spent an afternoon diagnosing a suite failure whose signature was `325 passed, 3 failures against an announced 607`. That exact sentence — the three numbers, the cancelled modules, and the statement gate as the cause — was already in the body of `a-new-lean-running-call-wired-past-env-makes-the-suite-slow-instead-of-red`, filed 2026-09-09T23:27:45Z, open and unclaimed the whole time.

IT WAS NOT A MISSED SEARCH, IT WAS A MISSED READ, TWICE OVER. Keel quoted that row's TITLE to Rowan at 14:25 as a candidate to work on, then hit its exact symptom at ~14:50 and did not connect them. Rowan had dumped every open row at session start, so the title rendered in Rowan's own terminal, and then spent the afternoon rediscovering the body from process listings and directory timestamps. Neither of us was ignorant of the row. We had both already put it on our screens.

THE BOARD'S FAILURE MODE IS NOT THAT ROWS ARE WRONG. It is that they are unfindable at the moment they would help. `bugs` filters by `--area` and `--severity`: the axes you use when BROWSING, when you have no symptom and are choosing what to work on. When a session is mid-failure it has the opposite thing — a literal artifact, an error string, a stack frame, a distinctive number — and nothing in the harness searches bodies for it.

WHY 'REMEMBER TO GREP THE BOARD' WILL NOT FIX IT: that is advice, and advice loses to a session in the middle of a live symptom, which is precisely the condition under which it failed for all three of us. It needs a verb and a moment.

THE VERB: `bugs search <text>`, case-insensitive over ids, titles and bodies, printing id, status and the matching line. This afternoon would have been thirty seconds. It is small and it has no dependencies.

THE MOMENT: not session start — a row read at session start is read before the symptom exists, which is exactly how both of us read past this one. The moment is when a session is SURPRISED. That belongs in the debugging habit as its first move, with the search string being the literal artifact and not a paraphrase of it: the number, the error text, the `file:line`. Every one of us had `325 passed, 3 failures` in hand and none of us typed it anywhere.

NOTE THE ASYMMETRY WITH CLAIMS. `/startup` already reports held claims, because a stale claim costs a peer. A row nobody can find costs a whole afternoon and there is no equivalent. The board is 111 rows of prose nobody adjudicates; its value is entirely in retrieval, and retrieval is the one thing it has no affordance for.

bugs.title: Five times in one day the answer was already on disk, correct, and reachable from nothing anyone reads
bugs.body:
Not missing information. Information PRESENT, CORRECT, and pointed at by nothing — so it is rediscovered from scratch, or its absence is inferred and acted on. Five instances on 2026-09-10, across three sessions:

1. THE BOARD ROW. `a-new-lean-running-call-wired-past-env-...`, filed 2026-09-09, open, contained the literal string `325 passed, 3 failures against an announced 607` and named the statement gate as the cause. Three sessions spent an afternoon rediscovering it. Keel quoted its TITLE at 14:25 as a candidate to work on; Rowan dumped every open row at session start and read past it in its own terminal. Neither was ignorant of the row.

2. THE CHECK FILES. `reverify --all` prints nothing until it finishes, so a death at node 60 of 116 appeared to leave nothing. But `verify` writes one check file per node into `harness/build/checks/`, as it goes, surviving the process — a complete per-node trail with a recoverable denominator. Rowan found it by looking for something else entirely.

3. THE annotate EVENT. Two attempts' `events.jsonl` carried `"written": false, "reason": "no statement to write: the check output had no #check line"` for two days, saying exactly what was wrong. Every downstream reader treated the resulting missing block as an accepted gap.

4. PARKED PROOFS — and this one comes with the project's own words for the defect attached. `dispatch.gleam:1344`, in what `status` already prints: "work already paid for that no verb points at, and an attempt whose outcome says `abandoned` is exactly the record nobody re-reads". Somebody saw the shape clearly enough to phrase it twice in one sentence and filed it as a fact about stray Lean files rather than as a pattern.

5. THE SKIPPED FIVE. `reverify --all` reported "116 of 116 re-verified, 0 needing attention" having silently not read five files. The report could not have said so: a skipped item is in no category, because an absence has no row. Caught by subtracting 77 from 82 — a command no ritual demanded.

WHY 'ADD A POINTER' IS THE WRONG FIX. It would have to be done five times, and there will be a sixth. The general form: EVERY ARTIFACT A SESSION PRODUCES SHOULD BE REACHABLE FROM SOMETHING A LATER SESSION ACTUALLY READS. In this harness that is `status`, `/startup`, and now `bugs search`. `status` already points at exactly one of the five.

TWO SPECIFIC FIXES THAT FALL OUT, each closing one instance and generalising:
- A long-running verb should stream one line per unit rather than buffering a report, so the output IS the progress and a death leaves a partial record with a countable denominator. Closes 2 and 5.
- A report should state what it ATTEMPTED alongside what it FOUND, reconciled by something outside the report. `reverify --all` said "116 re-verified" truthfully while reading 77 blocks and treating 5 as absent; both numbers were in the report and the GAP was not.

RELATED, and it is the retrieval half of the same thing: `the-board-is-searchable-by-area-and-severity-but-not-by-symptom`, whose verb `bugs search` now exists and closes instance 1.
bugs.resolution: 643c8e4 (Fathom): the cause, not the instances. Nobody forgot a pointer — A PRODUCER WITH NO READER IS NOT AN ERROR STATE, IT IS SILENCE: nothing fails, nothing warns, nothing is even slow, so the system's response to the defect is identical to its response to everything being fine. That is why all six filed instances were found by someone looking for something else; there was no other way to find them. So the fix follows from the cause: make 'produced and unread' a REPORTED state in a report a later session already reads. reach.gleam declares each artifact family against its reader and status prints it, so a family with artifacts and no reader prints as unread rather than not printing. The argument for status being the home was already in the codebase: stray_section calls its own family 'work already paid for that no verb points at' — the general case, written down and filed as a fact about Lean files. IT FOUND A SEVENTH INSTANCE ON ITS FIRST RUN, verified before I believed my own table: docs/attacks, 14 theorist documents, 416 KB, whose only source mentions were the guard permitting the write and a doc comment. THE BACKSTOP IS LOAD-BEARING: the family table is hand-maintained and will be forgotten, and a table that silently omits a family is this row's defect inside its own fix, so any docs/ directory no family declares prints as undeclared. TWO INSTANCES ALSO CLOSED CONCRETELY. docs/connections: 12 documents, 549 KB, one crystal visible to the seeder in two days; each document's own section 5 now reaches the seeder brief verbatim (32.7 KB, six percent — the measurement that dissolved Rowan's inline/index/distil fork rather than settling it), with the unfinished census document flagged rather than inlined, since inlining it silently would have shipped eleven good crystals and one confident blank. docs/attacks: two payload sections to two different readers — section 4 what-survived to the seeder, section 5 claims-that-died beside the obstructions file in the theorist and connector briefs, which is where the code said they belong rather than where I would have put them. Mapping 'section 5' across families would have carried killed routes to a seeder as candidates: a connector's section 5 is a handoff forward, a theorist's is the graveyard. THE MEASURED CONSEQUENCE, weighted as Rowan corrected it rather than as first offered: reachability is structural here, and his hand-distillation is the control group showing it was not. What the P2 seeder demonstrates is that a distilled crystal gets USED — cited by number in its own DOES NOT PROVE field, applied as a fence and not an invitation, taking the body rather than the headline — within hours of becoming reachable. NOT DONE, deliberately: nothing writes into docs/obstructions.md. The guard governs who may, a theorist is already told to append to it, and a mechanism that silently grows a curated file is the wrong kind of help. Suite 667/667 announced and passed, exit 0.

bugs.title: Nothing marks a proposal as landed, and the next seeder run overwrites the adjudication record
bugs.body:
Filed by Rowan on 2026-09-10 from session rule30-38, after landing all six of the 2026-09-09 seeder's proposals. Found at checkpoint, not during the work.

`blueprint/proposals/next.json` still lists all six proposals. All six are on the DAG. Nothing in the file, and no verb, distinguishes a proposal that has been LANDED from one still awaiting adjudication. The captain lands by hand -- writing statements into Rule30/Statements.lean and nodes into blueprint/dag.json -- and there is no `seed land`, so nothing ever writes back to the proposal file.

TWO CONSEQUENCES, and the second is the quiet one.
First, a captain reading next.json tomorrow cannot tell what is outstanding. Re-landing is not catastrophic -- a duplicate declaration in Statements.lean fails loudly, and duplicate node ids would be caught -- but the reader has to reconstruct the answer by cross-checking six ids against dag.json, which is exactly the check nobody performs on a file that looks settled.
Second, the path is a FIXED `next.json`. The next seeder run overwrites it. At that moment the record of what was proposed, what the automatic check said about each route, and which ones a captain accepted is gone from the one place a captain looks. It survives only in runs/<run-id>/seed-1/, which is a directory nobody re-reads -- and today's evidence is that this project loses things exactly there.

THIS IS AN INSTANCE OF `an-artifact-that-answers-the-question-exists-and-nothing-points-at-it` (6c338fb) and should be read beside it rather than alone: the adjudication record exists, is correct, and is pointed at by nothing that outlives the next seeder run.

WHAT WOULD FIX IT, cheapest first. (1) A `landed` field per proposal, written by whatever a captain runs when landing -- which today is nothing, so this implies (2). (2) A `seed land` verb doing what I did by hand: append the statement inside `namespace Statements`, add the node, and mark the proposal landed. That would also have caught two things I only caught because I checked -- that the seeded name must resolve as `Statements.<name>` under `type_of%`, and that this check reads the BUILT olean, so it gives a false negative against a stale one unless `lake build Rule30.Statements` runs first. (3) Failing both, date the file (`next-<date>.json`) so a new seeder cannot overwrite an unadjudicated one.

NOT URGENT AND NOT A BLOCKER: the six landed correctly and the board is consistent. This is about the next captain, and about the seeder run after this one.

bugs.title: dag.Node has no route field, so a route the captain verified at landing cannot reach the prover
bugs.body:
Filed by Rowan on 2026-09-10 from session rule30-38, immediately after landing the onset tier at f8d5e46 and watching it happen.

THE SHAPE. A seeder proposal carries an optional `route` (tactics plus imports) and the seed check adjudicates it. A captain reviews the proposal, verifies the route against the real definitions, and lands the statement. At that point the route is DISCARDED: dag.Node (src/harness/dag.gleam:137-156) has id, region, lean_name, description, deps, status, size, proof_file, attempts, verified, claimed_by, claimed_at, claimed_run, object, under, research -- and no route. The only field that reaches the prover brief and could carry one is `description`, which is free prose also read by the seeder brief and the index, so a tactic script there is a misuse rather than a home.

WHAT IT COST TONIGHT, MEASURED. I landed four statements for which I had personally elaborated four routes against the real definitions, each `#print axioms` clean (explorer/rowan_review_20260910.lean and explorer/rowan_routecheck/). Dispatch at the haiku rung, run 20260910T171512Z: rowNat_testBit_zero proved for $0.22 in 10 turns; rowNat_agree_forward budget_exhausted at 41 turns for $1.05, then proved on sonnet in 11 turns for $1.04; leftDiagonal_onset_le_not_of_black_ladder budget_exhausted at 41 turns for $1.01. So $2.06 and 82 turns went on rediscovering two proofs that were sitting in the captain's working directory at the moment of dispatch. The bug is not that the provers were bad. It is that nothing could hand them what was already known.

WHY THIS IS NOT SEEDING A HINT. CLAUDE.md's objection is real and I am not proposing to weaken it: an unverified route misdirects in a captain's voice to a model with no standing to doubt it, and forecloses a search a stronger model would win. That objection is about UNVERIFIED routes. A route the captain has elaborated is a different object -- not a hint about where to look, but a proof that exists. The field would need to encode exactly that distinction: carried only when checked, where checked means a command someone ran rather than a claim someone made.

WHAT WOULD FIX IT. A captain-set optional field on dag.Node, encoded only when present and round-tripped unvalidated, exactly as `under` was added (see the-board-does-not-record-which-wall-a-block-attacks, and 43cf4aa for `object` before it). Carrying the tactic text, its imports, and the moment it was verified, so a stale route is visibly stale. The prover brief then renders it under a heading saying what it is and what it is not: a proof that elaborated at landing, offered so the session need not rebuild it, NOT a constraint on how the node must be proved -- the harness still verifies whatever the prover actually writes, and a prover who finds a better proof should write that instead. The seeder's proposal `route` is already the right shape to land from, so the landing step becomes copying a field rather than dropping one.

ONE THING TO GET RIGHT, and it is why the field should carry its verification moment rather than a bare boolean. A route is a fact about a statement, and if the statement is later edited the route may stop closing it. A route that silently stops being true is the Checked type block problem one level out, and `reverify` is the existing precedent for the answer. See also the glossary section on quoting a measurement without its clock.

RELATED, and the reason this row is worth more than it looks: a-pre-indented-route-is-reported-as-not-closing-because-check-source-adds-two-spaces. That row means routes are currently reported dead when they are alive -- all four of tonight's seeder routes close when reassembled with the indentation the seeder actually wrote. So the pipeline today both mislabels good routes AND has nowhere to put the ones a captain rescues by hand. Fixing either alone leaves the value on the floor.

bugs.title: prove_one has no injectable twin, so one test runs real Lean against cfg.repo_root and a worktree suite starts a from-scratch Mathlib build
bugs.body:
Filed by Rowan on 2026-09-10 from session rule30-38. THE DESIGN IS KEEL'S, described to me in a peer message and deliberately not started at the end of a long session; it is on the board rather than in that message because a paragraph nobody can search is not a plan. Unclaimed.

THE MECHANISM, read at the call site rather than inferred. `verify.statement_resolves` has TWO call sites reachable from the suite, and they point at different Lean projects.

(1) `verify_test.gleam:400` and `:427` pass `lean_fixture.built()`. That is `test/fixture-project`, dependency-free, builds from nothing in about two seconds. `lean_fixture.gleam:14-17` says the path is derived from where the runner started and NEVER from `HARNESS_REPO_ROOT`, and `root()` reads `simplifile.current_directory()` with no env lookup. So for these tests the variable does nothing and cannot.

(2) `run_test.gleam:486` calls `dispatch.prove_one(f.cfg, id)`, and `dispatch.gleam:117` is `statement_gate(cfg, ...)`, which is `statement_resolves(cfg.repo_root, ...)`. The fixture config at `run_test.gleam:140-157` redirects shim, dag_path, bugs_path, runs_root, roster_path, agents_dir, stop_path, guard_port and turn_timeout_ms -- and NOT `repo_root`. The comment on those lines says why in as many words: `repo_root` stays the live checkout, it is where `.lake` is.

So exactly one Lean call in the suite points at the REAL project, and it is the one that hurts. In a fresh worktree with no `HARNESS_REPO_ROOT` set, `cfg.repo_root` is the worktree, the worktree has no `.lake`, and `lake build Rule30.Statements` there starts fetching Mathlib. That is the hours-long build found running with a dead parent on 2026-09-10 (see `an-orphaned-lake-build-outlives-the-suite-that-spawned-it`), and it is the slow call that trips the eunit module abort (see `one-slow-lean-test-aborts-its-whole-module-and-the-pass-line-looks-healthy`), which then reports a healthy-looking pass line over roughly half a suite.

WHY THIS IS `blocks` AND NOT FRICTION. CLAUDE.md's `Changing the framework` section prescribes worktrees for all framework work, and its suite bullet says `gleam test` from a worktree `needs no HARNESS_REPO_ROOT ... and is never required`. On the mechanism above that sentence is false, and false in the expensive direction: an agent following the file exactly, in the tree the same file tells them to work in, starts a from-scratch Mathlib build and then reads a pass line that looks fine. This is not a stale doc. It is a documented instruction that causes the failure, and it has now caught at least one agent who had no way to know better.

AND A WARNING IS DEMONSTRABLY NOT ENOUGH. On the same day, the agent who spent the afternoon establishing the cold-start abort, wrote it into `docs/glossary.md`, filed two rows about it and warned another agent by name against exactly this configuration, then created a fresh worktree and started a suite in it four hours later. Their own account, volunteered. That is the argument for a structural fix over better documentation: the best available warning, in the author's own words, four hours old, did not hold.

WHAT WOULD FIX IT, Keel's design. Give `prove_one` an injectable twin the way `run` has `run_with`, so `run_test` stubs the statement gate like its eight siblings already stub their own Lean-running dependencies (`Env` carries injectable fields for `verifier`, `check_proposals` and `sweep_strays` for exactly this reason, each with a doc comment saying so). Then NO Lean is invoked from a worktree at all, the fixture project covers what needs real elaboration, and both `HARNESS_REPO_ROOT` and the CLAUDE.md sentence stop being needed rather than being corrected.

SCOPE, from Keel: one function's signature and eight call sites in `run_test`. Small in lines, wide in blast radius, which is why it wants a session that is fresh rather than one that is ending.

WHAT IT CLOSES. This row, `one-slow-lean-test-aborts-its-whole-module-and-the-pass-line-looks-healthy`, and `an-orphaned-lake-build-outlives-the-suite-that-spawned-it` -- and it makes the CLAUDE.md sentence true again instead of requiring an edit.

THE INTERIM MITIGATION, with its scope stated honestly rather than as a cure: `HARNESS_REPO_ROOT=<the shared checkout> gleam test` removes the only Lean call in the suite that can trigger a from-scratch Mathlib build. One trial, 653 announced and 653 passed from a genuinely cold worktree. It does NOT rule out load as an independent trigger of the same abort -- the 325-of-607 run happened beside three provers and a seeder, and the green one beside two provers. Both mechanisms are real and neither excludes the other. Read the ANNOUNCED total before the pass count either way.

RELATED: `a-new-lean-running-call-wired-past-env-makes-the-suite-slow-instead-of-red`, which is this same defect's sibling -- three times in one evening a new Lean-running call went straight into dispatch.gleam instead of through `Env`, and the suite rather than review was what noticed.
bugs.resolution: c5172e5 and 30995f4, landed at 9dc2f07 with the CLAUDE.md flip at 760ea4f (Keel): prove_one built its live behaviour inline, so a test of it could stub nothing — and run_test deliberately leaves repo_root on the real checkout because that is where .lake is, so the statement gate shelled 'lake build Rule30.Statements' there. In a worktree with no .lake that one call starts building Mathlib from scratch: hours, outliving the suite, far past eunit's 50s per-test budget, and eunit cancels the whole module, so ~289 tests vanished behind a healthy-looking '325 passed, 3 failures'. prove_one_with(cfg, node_id, env_for) is the twin, as run_with is to run; all five inline behaviours now route through Env (statement gate, worker deps, index write, proposal check, stray sweep) and prove_one is a thin wrapper supplying live_env. It takes fn(log.Log) -> Env rather than an Env because live_env closes over the run log and the log must not open until validation passes — a bad node id should leave no run directory. index_proof now takes the index function so the 'index' event still reaches the attempt log; a naive swap to env.index would have dropped it silently. CLOSURE TEST in the configuration that used to break: genuinely cold worktree, no .lake, NO HARNESS_REPO_ROOT — announced 653, 653 passed, exit 0, and no .lake was created afterwards, so no Mathlib build started at all. Predicted 653 from an on-disk count before running. Suite over the merge: 667 announced, 667 passed. The variable is no longer required and CLAUDE.md says so again truthfully; both halves landed together so the file was never lying in either direction. Note for the reachability row: run_test's env() helper already contained the statement_gate stub that fixes this, already carried a comment diagnosing it, and was ACTIVELY IN USE by the eight run tests beside it on every suite run — three lines from the calls that could not reach it, for want of one parameter.

bugs.title: seed check cannot verify a route whose imports name a proof file for another node in the same tier
bugs.body:
Filed by Rowan on 2026-09-10 from session rule30-38, from run 20260910T220756Z.

THE SHAPE. A seeder proposed six nodes as a tier, where later nodes' routes import the proof files of earlier nodes in the SAME tier -- which is exactly how a tier is supposed to be structured, since the whole point of a tier is that its members build on one another. Three of the six then failed the route check with:

  error: object file '...\.lake\build\lib\lean\Rule30\Proofs\Rule30AlternatingStep.olean' of module Rule30.Proofs.Rule30AlternatingStep does not exist

The named modules are the proof files of `rule30_alternating_step` and `column_black_run_of_alternating`, both proposed in the same document and neither landed, so neither has a proof file. The route may be perfectly good and there is no way to find out.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS. The route check is the only adjudicator of a route, and its verdict is what a captain lands on. A route that CANNOT be checked is reported in the same column as a route that was checked and failed -- `DOES NOT CLOSE` -- so the report collapses 'this is wrong' and 'I could not tell', which is the third-outcome collapse this project's own glossary has a section about. Tonight it hid three routes of six.

It also penalises exactly the proposals we most want. A tier whose members are independent gets clean verdicts; a tier that builds a chain -- the shape a decomposition is supposed to have -- gets its later members marked unverifiable. That is backwards.

WHAT WOULD FIX IT. Check the tier in dependency order in one scratch project: elaborate each proposal's statement as an axiom or a `sorry`-ed theorem in a generated module named the way its landed proof file would be, so a sibling's import resolves to the STATEMENT rather than to a proof. That is sound for a route check, which asks whether the tactics close the goal given its hypotheses, not whether the dependencies are proved. A cheaper first step, if that is too much: report a third verdict, `NOT CHECKABLE (imports an unlanded sibling)`, distinct from `DOES NOT CLOSE`, so a captain can tell the two apart at a glance.

RELATED: `a-pre-indented-route-is-reported-as-not-closing-because-check-source-adds-two-spaces` (fixed 2026-09-10) was the same class -- a good route reported dead -- and the lesson there was that a manufactured `DOES NOT CLOSE` is indistinguishable from a real one. This is that lesson again from a different cause.

bugs.title: Four routes across two seeder passes failed with `unknown tactic`, cause unknown
bugs.body:
Filed by Rowan on 2026-09-10 from session rule30-38. FILED AS AN OBSERVATION, NOT A DIAGNOSIS: I could not find the cause in reasonable time and stopped rather than rabbit-hole it. Whoever takes this starts from zero, not from my theory, because I do not have one that survived.

THE SYMPTOM. Four routes, across runs 20260910T212409Z and 20260910T220756Z, failed the route check with `error: unknown tactic` at a specific line and column -- for example `rule30_alternating_step ... :17:5: error: unknown tactic` and `column_one_succ_of_white ... :6:3: error: unknown tactic`.

WHAT I RULED OUT. It is NOT the indentation defect fixed earlier the same day (`a-pre-indented-route-is-reported-as-not-closing-because-check-source-adds-two-spaces`, closed against b95bd06): that fix is landed, and I checked the offending route's bytes directly with `repr` -- in the `rule30_alternating_step` case the `cases ... with` arms `| zero =>` and `| succ n =>` are both at exactly four spaces, so they are consistent with each other and the common-margin normalisation preserves that.
